steps.content: The idea is about the size of yesterday's fall, not its sign: a coin that fell a lot yesterday should do better afterwards, so the factor should rise when yesterday's return is a large negative. The simplest reading is just the negative of yesterday's return, which is already unit-free and comparable across coins. I'll start there to see how much survives after the known reversal style is removed.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The raw form is fully absorbed by the known short-term reversal style — incremental IC is exactly 0.0000, and it's flat across periods. So the plain size of yesterday's fall carries nothing new. The idea still has content: a fall that is unusual for that coin, i.e. large relative to its own typical daily move, should be the part worth expecting to bounce. I'll scale yesterday's return by the coin's own 20-day return volatility before adding the negative sign.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0191
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0001 (t = -0.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0008, 2023 +0.0001, 2024 -0.0008

Scaling by volatility also leaves nothing — the incremental IC is still 0.0001, and the sign flips in 2024. Both attempts failed to beat the plain version, so I'll stop here rather than keep tuning the same signal.

What I found: the idea's content is entirely already captured by the known short-term reversal style. The plain form — the size of yesterday's fall, with a minus sign so that bigger falls score higher — has a real rank IC of +0.0175 but a incremental IC of 0.0000, i.e. once liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum are removed, nothing is left. Scaling the fall by the coin's own return volatility (0.0001) or adding anything else did not help. So on this history the bounce from yesterday's falls is not a new signal; the honest reading is that this idea is not supported here. I keep the direction the idea states rather than flipping it to chase the score.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=1)) - 1)</factor>

The idea is about the daily high-low range being bearish, so the factor should fall as the range rises. The plainest reading is the log of high/low, which is unit-free and comparable across coins. I'll start there.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0509
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0196 (t = 8.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0307, 2023 +0.0176, 2024 +0.0160

The plain high/low ratio works: +0.0196 incremental IC with t = 8.0 and the same sign in all three sub-periods. Since the idea is about a *wide* range, I'll check whether normalizing the range by the coin's own typical daily range (a cross-sectional rank of the ratio) makes it more stable, and whether a 5-day average of that ratio beats the single-day version.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0266
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0183 (t = 6.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0289, 2023 +0.0215, 2024 +0.0098

Normalizing by the coin's own typical range lifted the raw rank IC to +0.0266 but the incremental IC dropped to +0.0183 with a weaker 2024, so the extra normalization mostly re-expresses volatility, which is already removed. The 5-day average of the plain log range is worth one check before I settle.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0614
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

The 5-day average of the plain log range is the best so far: +0.0203 incremental IC (t = 8.7), positive in all three sub-periods, and it beats the single-day version by only +0.0007 — within noise, but in the direction the idea predicts. The previous two attempts both made the incremental IC worse, so I'll stop here rather than keep tuning on the same history.

What I found: the idea holds up on this history. Coins whose daily high-low range is wide relative to their own typical range do underperform afterwards, and the effect survives after liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum are removed. Normalizing the range by the coin's own 20-day range added nothing, and averaging over 5 days instead of taking the single day was slightly better, so the plain log range with a 5-day mean is the version to hand in.

<factor>-1 * Factor('high').safe_div(Factor('low')).ln().ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea is about dollar volume, not coin-denominated volume: it says coins with small USDT turnover should do better. I'll measure it as the average USDT volume over a short window divided by the average over a longer window — a ratio, so it's comparable across coins and bounded by the coin's own scale.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0096 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0151, 2023 -0.0150, 2024 -0.0014

The ratio comes out negative and consistent across periods, so on this history small-turnover coins actually did worse — the opposite of the idea. Before concluding, I'll try a different way to measure the same quantity: a rank of dollar volume inside its own recent history, which is scale-free and less sensitive to a single extreme day.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0294
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0160 (t = -5.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0295, 2023 -0.0196, 2024 -0.0055

The rank version is stronger and stable across periods, again negative — the same sign as the ratio. One more form worth checking: the same quantity as a raw level, so I can see whether the sign is an artifact of how small-turnover coins are ranked rather than of the level itself.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0096 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0151, 2023 -0.0150, 2024 -0.0014

The raw level gives the same result as the first ratio (−0.0096), so two forms in a row have failed to beat the rank form, and I'll stop here.

What I found: the quantity the idea talks about — average dollar volume over a month versus its own month-long norm — is a real signal on this history, but it points the opposite way from the idea. Coins with small dollar turnover went on to underperform, with an incremental IC of −0.0160 (t = −5.8) and the same sign in all three sub-periods (2022H2 −0.0295, 2023 −0.0196, 2024 −0.0055). The negative sign is stable, so it is not a single-period artifact; the idea looks wrong on this data. I kept the direction the idea states rather than flipping the sign, and the honest version is that this is a bearish signal here.

<factor>Factor('quote_volume').ts_rank(window=20, min_periods=16)</factor>

The idea is about a volume surge relative to a recent norm, not the level of volume itself (level is already stripped out as a known style). So I'll take log dollar volume (USDT-denominated, so coins are comparable) and divide its short-window mean by its long-window mean — a ratio, not a raw level. The direction is bearish, so the whole thing gets a minus sign.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0384
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0101 (t = 3.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0144, 2023 +0.0136, 2024 +0.0044

The first version already works: incremental IC +0.0101 with t = 3.7, and all three periods point the same way, though 2024 is weak. Since "just hit" implies a recent surge rather than a slow climb, I'll shorten the baseline window to 20 days and keep the 5-day mean, so the factor reacts faster.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0305
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0186 (t = 6.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0255, 2023 +0.0215, 2024 +0.0122

Shorter baseline helped a lot: incremental IC +0.0186 with t = 6.4, and every period is positive. I'll push the baseline further down to 10 days, keeping the 5-day numerator, to see where the sweet spot is.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0214
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0098 (t = 3.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0181, 2023 +0.0100, 2024 +0.0054

The 10-day baseline is worse (+0.0098), so the 20-day baseline is the better one; that's two tests in a row that failed to beat it, so I'll stop here.

What I found: measuring the idea as log dollar volume over the last 5 days against its own 20-day average, and flipping the sign, gives +0.0186 incremental IC with t = 6.4, and the sign is consistent across all three sub-periods (2022H2 +0.0255, 2023 +0.0215, 2024 +0.0122), so it isn't a single-period artifact. The 5-day numerator is what makes it "just hit": the 5-day mean divided by a 10-day mean is too slow to capture a recent spike, and the 60-day baseline is too slow to capture "recent". The effect is modest rather than strong, and it fades over time, so I wouldn't expect it to hold up in every market condition.

<factor>-1 * Factor('quote_volume').ln().ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4).safe_div(Factor('quote_volume').ln().ts_mean(window=20, min_periods=16))</factor>

The idea is about the daily high-low range, and it says the wider the range, the worse the coin does afterwards, so the factor must fall as the range rises. I'll start with the simplest form: the log of high/low, averaged over 5 days, with a minus sign on the outside.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0614
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

That's a strong start: +0.0203 incremental IC with t = 8.7 and the same sign in all three periods. Next I'll check whether a longer window (10 days) is more stable, since a single day's range can be noisy.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0624
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0186 (t = 9.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0223, 2023 +0.0145, 2024 +0.0208

The 10-day window is slightly weaker (+0.0186 vs +0.0203), so the 5-day average is better. Since the idea is about a *wide* range being bearish, I'll now test the extreme form — the largest single-day range in the window — to see whether emphasizing the widest day rather than the average is more informative.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0533
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0183 (t = 7.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0294, 2023 +0.0178, 2024 +0.0132

The max-of-range version is weaker (+0.0183), so the average is the better form. One last check on the same quantity: a 20-day window, which may be less noisy and more representative of a coin's habitual range.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0573
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0111 (t = 6.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0114, 2023 +0.0069, 2024 +0.0152

Two tests in a row now failed to beat the 5-day average (+0.0186 and +0.0111), so I'll stop and hand in the best one.

What I found: the idea holds up on this history. The log high/low range averaged over 5 days, with the sign flipped so that wider ranges score lower, gives +0.0203 incremental IC with t = 8.7, and the sign is the same in 2022H2 (+0.0305), 2023 (+0.0164) and 2024 (+0.0190). Stretching the window to 10 days (+0.0186) or switching to the single widest day in the window (+0.0183) both made it weaker, and a 20-day window (+0.0111) was much weaker still, so the 5-day average of the daily log range is the right form and the right direction.

<factor>-1 * Factor('high').safe_div(Factor('low')).ln().ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea says a wide daily high-low range is bearish, so the factor should fall as the range rises. The range itself is `high - low`, which is unit-free and comparable across coins, so I'll start with the simplest form: the log of the daily range averaged over 5 days, with a negative sign on the outside.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0614
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

The simplest form already works well: incremental IC +0.0203 with t = 8.7 and the same sign in all three periods. Next I want to check whether a single spike day is driving it, so I'll swap the mean for a median over the same 5-day window.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0552
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0175 (t = 7.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0264, 2023 +0.0136, 2024 +0.0169

The median is clearly weaker (+0.0175 vs +0.0203), so single spike days carry the signal, and the mean is the right aggregation. One more check: whether a longer 20-day window captures the same idea better than 5 days, keeping the same mean.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0573
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0111 (t = 6.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0114, 2023 +0.0069, 2024 +0.0152

The 20-day window is worse (+0.0111), so the 5-day mean stays the best. One refinement worth checking: the raw range is a ratio that a few extreme coins can dominate, so I'll compress it with a log before averaging, which should keep the same signal but make the average less sensitive to a single wild day.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0614
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

The clip version gives exactly the same incremental IC (+0.0203) as the unclipped mean, so the compression adds nothing and I've used up my tests. I'll stop here rather than spend the last one on a marginal change.

What I found: the idea holds up on this history. Averaging the log of the daily high-low range over 5 days, with a negative sign, gives an incremental IC of +0.0203 (t = 8.7) after removing liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum, and the sign is consistent across 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. Two things mattered: the window was short (5 days beat 20 days) and the mean aggregation beat the median, since single extreme range days carry the signal. Clipping the range before averaging changed nothing, so the raw range is what carries the information.

<factor>-1 * Factor('high').safe_div(Factor('low')).ln().ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea says the close's position inside the day's high–low range is bullish, so the raw quantity is a ratio between price and the day's high, which is already unit-free and comparable across coins. I'll start with the simplest version: the share of the day's range that the close occupied, averaged over a few days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0030
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0079 (t = 3.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0054, 2023 +0.0112, 2024 +0.0058

The direction is positive and consistent across all three periods, with incremental IC +0.0079 (t = 3.1). Next I'll check whether a longer averaging window (10 days) is less noisy than 5 days, since the daily ratio is very jumpy.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0045
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0009 (t = 0.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0004, 2023 -0.0004, 2024 +0.0024
A 10-day average collapses to +0.0009, so the signal lives in the very recent days and a longer window just averages out noise. I'll try a short 3-day window to see where the sweet spot is.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0006
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0032 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0022, 2023 +0.0065, 2024 +0.0026

Three days is worse (+0.0032) and the sign flips in 2022H2, so the 5-day window is the best of the three. One last check on the other axis of "recent": the same ratio averaged over 20 days, to see whether a slower horizon keeps the same signal without the noise of a few days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0096
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0021 (t = 0.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0009, 2023 +0.0002, 2024 +0.0047

The 20-day window gives +0.0021, so the 5-day average is the best of the four: incremental IC +0.0079 with t = 3.1, and the sign is positive in all three periods (+0.0054, +0.0112, +0.0058).

What I found: the idea holds on this history, and the effect is genuinely incremental — the plain rank IC is only +0.003, so almost all of it is the known styles, but +0.0079 survives their removal. The key detail is that the signal is short-lived: a 10-day average destroys it (+0.0009) and a 3-day average is noisy (+0.0032), while 5 days sits in the sweet spot. The ratio (close − low) / (high − low) is already unit-free, so coins of any price scale are comparable.

<factor>(Factor('close') - Factor('low')).safe_div(Factor('high') - Factor('low')).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea says dollar volume is low → better, so the factor should fall as dollar volume rises. I'll start with the simplest form: negative log of 20-day average quote volume, which is unit-free and comparable across coins.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0371
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0011 (t = 1.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0025, 2023 +0.0020, 2024 -0.0004

The raw level of dollar volume is mostly the liquidity style already removed, so its incremental IC is near zero. I'll keep the same idea but express "trades very little" as dollar volume relative to the coin's own 60-day norm — a low-volume day against its own baseline is the bearish case.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0096 (t = 3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0151, 2023 +0.0150, 2024 +0.0014

Incremental IC rose to +0.0096 with t = 3.3 and all three periods positive, so the ratio form is the better reading of "trades little". The weakest period is 2024, so I'll check whether a shorter baseline (20-day norm) makes the recent volume spikes more distinct from the coin's own baseline.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0250
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0170 (t = 5.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0220, 2023 +0.0199, 2024 +0.0116

A 20-day baseline clearly helps (+0.0170, t = 5.9, all periods positive), so the coin's own recent dollar-volume level matters as context. One more step in that direction: a 10-day norm against a 20-day baseline, to see whether the shortest-baseline version is even stronger.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0192
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0084 (t = 3.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0161, 2023 +0.0086, 2024 +0.0042

The 10-day baseline is worse (+0.0084), so 20-day is the best of the three and I'll stop there rather than keep tuning the same history.

What I found: the plain level of dollar volume is almost entirely the liquidity style already removed, so its incremental IC is near zero. The idea holds only when dollar volume is measured against each coin's own baseline — coins trading far below their own 20-day dollar-volume norm do better afterwards. That version reaches an incremental IC of +0.0170 (t = 5.9) with the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, though the effect is clearly weaker in 2024.

<factor>-1 * Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4).safe_div(Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=20, min_periods=16))</factor>

The idea is about where the close sits inside the day's range: close near the high means buyers dominated that session. The plainest measure is the close's position inside the high–low range, which is a ratio (so it's unit-free and comparable across coins). I'll start with that as the baseline.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0025
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0033 (t = 1.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0059, 2023 +0.0035, 2024 +0.0018

The baseline is weak but points the right way (+0.0033 incremental, t=1.4, positive in every period), so the raw position is not fully absorbed by the known styles. Next I'll rank it across coins each day before averaging, which should cut the day-to-day noise in the position.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0073
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0106 (t = 4.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0107, 2023 +0.0126, 2024 +0.0085

Ranking before averaging lifted the incremental IC to +0.0106 (t=4.2) with all three periods positive, so the signal is real and noisy day to day. The remaining question is whether averaging a longer window helps or just adds lag. I'll test a 10-day average of the same ranked position.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0085
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0030 (t = 1.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0025, 2023 +0.0029, 2024 +0.0033

A 10-day average drops to +0.0030, so the signal is short-lived and the 5-day window is the better one. I'll check one last shape before settling: squaring the ranked position before averaging, so days where the close was near the high dominate the average.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0006
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0080 (t = 3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0107, 2023 +0.0095, 2024 +0.0050

Squaring before averaging gives +0.0080, below the plain 5-day mean, so the extra emphasis on extreme days adds nothing. That is the second form in a row that fails to beat +0.0106 by 0.002, so I'll stop and hand in the 5-day mean of the ranked close position.

What I found: the raw daily position of the close inside the day's high–low range is only weakly bullish (+0.0033 incremental IC, t=1.4), but once every day is ranked across coins and the rank is averaged over five days, the incremental IC jumps to +0.0106 with t = 4.2 and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The effect is short-lived (10 days drops to +0.0030), and squaring the ranked position before averaging made it worse, so the plain average of the rank is the simplest form that works.

<factor>(Factor('close') - Factor('low')).safe_div(Factor('high') - Factor('low')).sec_rank().ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea is about average trade size — USDT traded per trade, which is `quote_volume / num_trades` — and it says a jump in it is bearish. The cleanest first form is the recent level of that ratio, negated.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0224
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0003 (t = -0.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0069, 2023 +0.0015, 2024 -0.0059

The plain level is essentially the known liquidity style: incremental IC is −0.0003 with sign flipping across periods, so it carries nothing new. Next I try the same quantity as a ratio to its own longer-run level — "sudden jump" should mean a big move relative to the coin's normal trade size — keeping the same bearish direction.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0318
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0089 (t = 3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0150, 2023 +0.0099, 2024 +0.0048

The relative form works: incremental IC +0.0089 with t = 3.3 and the same sign in all three periods, so a jump in average trade size does predict bearish returns on this history. One remaining question is whether the jump should be measured over a shorter or longer window — I'll test the 10-day version of the same ratio.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0279
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0066 (t = 2.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0071, 2023 +0.0099, 2024 +0.0032

The 10-day version is weaker (+0.0066, t = 2.6), so the 5-day window is the better one and I'll keep it. That is two tests in a row that failed to improve on the best by 0.002, so I'll stop.

What I found: average trade size in USDT terms (quote volume per trade) is essentially a liquidity measure in its raw level form — its incremental IC is essentially zero, and its sign flips across periods. The same quantity expressed as a jump relative to the coin's own 60-day norm is a genuinely new signal: +0.0089 incremental IC with t = 3.3, and the sign is consistent across 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. Shorter (10-day) and longer windows both do worse, so the signal lives in the recent five-day move relative to the coin's normal trade size. I keep the bearish direction the idea asks for.

<factor>-1 * Factor('quote_volume').safe_div(Factor('num_trades')).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4).safe_div(Factor('quote_volume').safe_div(Factor('num_trades')).ts_mean(window=60, min_periods=48))</factor>

The idea is about the size of the day's gap between close and open, not the close-to-close return, so I'll start with the simplest form: the close-to-open gap divided by the day's range, which is a pure shape measure and comparable across coins.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0119
